Scheiner would rather see the nation adopt a single-payer system like the ones in Canada and Europe. The benefits, advocates say, is that pricey administrative costs are cut, resulting in large savings to patients. It's something that an up-and-coming coming state Sen. Obama talked about  six years ago. "I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan. ... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House," Obama said in 2003. But that position evolved during the campaign. "If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we're not starting from scratch," Obama said in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008. Now, the president favors giving Americans the option of joining a government-run plan that would compete with private insurers.  Watch more on the health care debate » . "Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that," Obama said in Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday. But Scheiner says that nobody has seen the details of that option, making it a hard sell for the president. "We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be. If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself." Scheiner almost had a chance to confront the president with his concerns. He was invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, but he says he was dropped from the program. "I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words," he said. "We've got to do something better." Scheiner finally had a chance to have his say Thursday. He and other doctors who support a single-payer system gathered in Washington to meet with lawmakers and rally supporters. He may not be the president's doctor anymore, but Scheiner says he's trying to save the patient before it's too late. CNN's Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.

Keywords: WASHINGTON, CNN, President

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- President Obama frequently speaks about the many forces arrayed against his health care plan. Yet one critic has remained relatively quiet in the debate: Dr. David Scheiner, who served as President Obama’s personal physician for 22 years.

Scheiner, a Chicago, Illinois-based physician, has taken a close look at the president’s prescription for health care reform and believes it amounts to bad medicine.

“This isn’t that kind of health care program that I think is going to work,” he said.

What makes Scheiner’s view especially notable is his long relationship with Obama. He was the former Illinois senator’s personal physician for 22 years and voted for him in the 2008 presidential election.

Scheiner believes the president’s plan does not go far enough. In his view, the most troubling part of the proposal is that “private insurers continue to be a part of the health scheme.” Watch Scheiner talk about his objections »

“Everybody keeps saying we don’t want the government involved in health care,” Scheiner said in an interview. “But the government is involved in Medicare, and it works.”

Scheiner would prefer to see the United States adopt a single-payer system similar to those in Canada and Europe. Such a financing system relies on one “payer” — which could be a government-run agency — to cover all health care costs billed by doctors, hospitals and other health professionals. Advocates say the benefit is that costly administrative expenses are reduced, producing significant savings for patients.

It is an idea that then-state Sen. Obama discussed six years ago.

“I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan. ... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we’ve got to take back the White House, and we’ve got take back the Senate, and we’ve got to take back the House,” Obama said in 2003.

But that position evolved during the campaign.

“If I were designing a system from scratch, then I’d probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we’re not starting from scratch,” Obama said in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008.

Now, the president favors giving Americans the option of joining a government-run plan that would compete with private insurers. Watch more on the health care debate »

“Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I’m tired of hearing that,” Obama said Thursday in Raleigh, North Carolina.

But Scheiner says the details of that option remain unclear, making it a difficult proposal for the president to sell.

“We don’t even fully know what the public option is going to be. If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I’m not sure it will be able to support itself.”

Scheiner nearly had an opportunity to raise his concerns directly with the president. He was invited to a recent televised town hall meeting with Obama, but he says he was later dropped from the program.

“I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words,” he said. “We’ve got to do something better.”

Scheiner finally had a chance to make his case Thursday. He and other doctors who support a single-payer system gathered in Washington to meet with lawmakers and rally supporters.

He may no longer be the president’s doctor, but Scheiner says he is trying to save the patient before it is too late.

CNN’s Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — President Obama frequently points to the many groups and individuals opposing his health care proposal. Yet one opponent has stayed mostly quiet during the national argument: Dr. David Scheiner, who served as Obama’s personal doctor for 22 years.

Scheiner, a physician based in Chicago, Illinois, has examined Obama’s approach to health care reform and believes it is the wrong remedy. “This isn't that kind of health care program that I think is going to work,” he said.

What gives Scheiner’s criticism added weight is his long history with Obama. He treated Obama for 22 years and supported the former Illinois senator in the 2008 presidential election. Even so, Scheiner argues that the president’s proposal is not ambitious enough. To him, the biggest flaw is that “private insurers continue to be a part of the health scheme.”

Scheiner said in an interview that he rejects the argument that government should stay out of health care. “Everybody keeps saying we don't want the government involved in health care,” he said. “But the government is involved in Medicare, and it works.”

Instead, Scheiner favors a single-payer model similar to systems used in Canada and Europe. Under that kind of arrangement, one payer — potentially a government agency — covers health care expenses submitted by doctors, hospitals and other medical providers. Supporters say such a system reduces expensive administrative costs, producing major savings for patients.

Obama himself discussed that idea six years earlier, when he was a rising state senator. In 2003, he said, “I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care plan. ... But as all of you know, we may not get there immediately, because first we've got to take back the White House, and we've got take back the Senate, and we've got to take back the House.”

During the presidential campaign, however, Obama’s position shifted. Speaking in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in August 2008, he said, “If I were designing a system from scratch, then I'd probably set up a single-payer system. But the problem is we're not starting from scratch.”

As president, Obama now supports creating a government-run insurance option that Americans could choose, which would compete alongside private insurance companies. In Raleigh, North Carolina, on Thursday, he pushed back against critics who describe the idea as a government takeover. “Nobody is talking about some government takeover of health care. I'm tired of hearing that,” he said.

Scheiner argues that the public still lacks key information about what that government option would actually look like, which makes it difficult for Obama to win support. “We don't even fully know what the public option is going to be,” he said. “If the public option is too good, patients who are sick will flock to it, and I'm not sure it will be able to support itself.”

Scheiner nearly had an opportunity to raise his objections directly with Obama. He was invited to take part in a recent televised town hall with the president, but he said he was later removed from the program. “I just hope that the Congress, the American public and the president will hear some of my words,” he said. “We've got to do something better.”

On Thursday, Scheiner finally got a forum to express his views. He joined other doctors who back a single-payer system in Washington, where they met with lawmakers and rallied supporters.

Although Scheiner is no longer Obama’s physician, he says his goal is still to help save the patient before it is too late.

CNN’s Ed Hornick and Brittany Cummings contributed to this report.
outputs.L3:
Dr. David Scheiner, who served as President Barack Obama’s personal physician for 22 years, publicly criticized Obama’s health care reform plan, arguing that it did not go far enough to fix the problems in the American health care system. Although Obama’s proposal was presented as a major reform effort, Scheiner believed it was too limited and failed to address the deeper structural issues that make health care expensive and difficult to access for many people.

According to Scheiner, the plan’s greatest weakness was that it continued to leave private insurance companies at the center of the health care system. In his view, a reform plan that preserves such a large role for private insurers cannot fully solve problems such as high costs, complicated billing, and unequal access to care. He argued that as long as private insurers remain central, the system will continue to be driven in part by profit motives rather than solely by patient care.

Scheiner instead supports a single-payer health care system, similar to those used in countries such as Canada and in parts of Europe. Under a single-payer model, the government typically finances health care, while doctors and hospitals may remain private. Scheiner pointed to Medicare as evidence that government involvement in health care can work effectively in the United States. For him, expanding the logic of Medicare to cover everyone would be a more efficient and fair solution than relying on a patchwork of private insurance plans.

Supporters of single-payer health care argue that such systems can reduce administrative costs by simplifying the way medical bills are processed and paid. Instead of dealing with many different insurance companies, each with its own rules, forms, and payment procedures, providers would work within a more unified system. Advocates say this could generate significant savings, which could then be passed on to patients through lower costs, broader coverage, and improved access to care.

Obama himself had previously expressed support for single-payer health care. In 2003, before his presidential campaign, he spoke favorably about the idea. However, during his run for president, his position shifted toward a more incremental approach that sought to expand coverage while preserving a major role for private insurance companies. This shift disappointed single-payer advocates like Scheiner, who believed that the reform plan missed an important opportunity to create a simpler, more universal health care system.

**Obama’s former doctor says health reform plan doesn’t go far enough**

*By [Reporter Name]*

President Barack Obama’s former personal physician is criticizing the administration’s health care reform plan, saying it falls short of the sweeping changes needed to fix the nation’s medical system.

Dr. David Scheiner, a Chicago-based physician who treated Obama for more than two decades before he entered the White House, has said the president’s proposal relies too heavily on private insurance companies and does not do enough to control costs or guarantee universal coverage.

Scheiner has been an outspoken supporter of a single-payer health care system, often described as “Medicare for all,” in which the government would finance health care coverage for Americans while medical care would continue to be delivered by doctors and hospitals.

“I don’t think this goes far enough,” Scheiner has said of Obama’s approach, arguing that expanding coverage through a mix of private insurance regulations, subsidies and public programs leaves too many of the current system’s problems intact.

The Obama administration has defended its reform plan as a politically achievable effort to expand insurance coverage, prevent insurers from denying coverage based on pre-existing conditions and make health care more affordable for families and businesses.

But Scheiner and other single-payer advocates argue that the legislation would preserve a fragmented system with high administrative costs and continued reliance on private insurers. They contend that a government-run financing model would be more efficient and equitable.

Obama has previously acknowledged that a single-payer system might be simpler in theory but has said transitioning the United States away from its existing employer-based and private insurance system would be too disruptive. Instead, he has backed reforms designed to build on the current system while expanding access to care.

The criticism from Scheiner highlights a broader divide among Democrats and health care advocates: whether reform should focus on incremental changes to the existing system or pursue a more fundamental restructuring.

For supporters of the president’s plan, the legislation represents the most significant health care overhaul in decades. For critics like Scheiner, it is a missed opportunity to create a universal system that treats health care as a guaranteed right.

Scheiner, a supporter of a single-payer system similar to Medicare for all Americans, said the administration’s approach would expand coverage but leave in place what he views as the core problem in U.S. health care: a profit-driven insurance industry that adds administrative costs and can limit patients’ access to care.

The criticism is notable because Scheiner cared for Obama for more than two decades in Chicago and has previously spoken favorably about the president personally. But on health policy, he has broken sharply with the White House, saying Obama’s plan represents a political compromise rather than the comprehensive overhaul he believes is needed.

Obama’s proposal seeks to broaden coverage, regulate insurers more tightly and create new options for individuals and small businesses to buy health plans. The president has argued that his plan would protect people with existing coverage while helping the uninsured obtain affordable care.

Scheiner said that approach is inadequate. By keeping private insurers in the system, he argued, the plan would continue to burden doctors and patients with bureaucracy and would not achieve the savings or universal coverage promised by advocates of deeper reform.

The White House has defended its strategy as the most practical path through Congress, where a single-payer plan has little support among lawmakers. Administration officials have said the proposal would curb abusive insurance practices, reduce costs over time and bring millions of uninsured Americans into the system.

Scheiner’s comments highlight a broader divide among Democrats and health care advocates: whether to pursue sweeping structural change through a government-run system or to build on the existing mix of private and public coverage. For liberals who wanted Obama to champion single-payer health care, the president’s plan remains a disappointment — and, in Scheiner’s words, “bad medicine.”

counterfactuals.output:
**Health Care Debate: Why Obama’s Former Doctor Backed Single-Payer — and Rejected the Public Option**

In the heat of the national health care debate, one voice drew particular attention: Dr. David Scheiner, a Chicago physician who had treated Barack Obama before his presidency. Scheiner publicly argued that the reform proposals being advanced by the Obama administration did not go far enough. His preferred solution was not a public option added to the existing insurance market, but a true single-payer health care system.

The distinction matters.

A **public option** would create a government-run insurance plan to compete alongside private insurers. Americans could choose it, but private insurance companies would remain central to the system. A **single-payer system**, by contrast, would replace most private insurance with one publicly financed plan covering everyone, similar in broad concept to Medicare for all.

Scheiner’s argument was straightforward: the American health care system was too fragmented, too expensive, and too dominated by private insurance interests to be fixed with modest reforms.

He believed that keeping private insurers at the center of the system would preserve many of the problems reform was supposed to solve — high administrative costs, complicated billing, gaps in coverage, and denial of care based on cost or coverage rules.

Supporters of the public option said it would inject competition into the insurance market. If private companies charged too much or offered weak coverage, a government plan could pressure them to improve. For many Democrats at the time, the public option was seen as a politically realistic compromise: more ambitious than insurance regulation alone, but less disruptive than replacing the private insurance system altogether.

Scheiner disagreed. He saw the public option as an inadequate half-measure.

From his perspective, a public plan competing inside a private insurance marketplace would not solve the underlying structural problem. Private insurers could still select healthier customers, market aggressively to lower-risk groups, and leave the public plan with older or sicker patients. That, critics warned, could make the public option more expensive and politically vulnerable.

Scheiner also objected to the administrative complexity of a mixed system. In a single-payer model, hospitals and doctors would deal with one primary payer and one simplified set of rules. In a public-option model, providers would still face multiple insurers, different billing systems, varying coverage standards, and layers of bureaucracy.

His case was also moral as much as economic. He argued that health care should be treated as a right, not as a product dependent on employment, income, or the rules of an insurance company. A universal Medicare-style system, he believed, would guarantee coverage to every American while giving the government greater power to control costs.

The Obama administration, however, pursued a different path. The Affordable Care Act ultimately expanded coverage through Medicaid, subsidies, insurance exchanges, and new rules on private insurers. The public option itself was dropped before final passage.

For Scheiner and other single-payer advocates, that outcome confirmed their concern: once reform was built around preserving the private insurance industry, the final law would inevitably be limited.

The debate highlighted a major divide within the Democratic coalition. Some reformers prioritized political feasibility and incremental expansion of coverage. Others, like Scheiner, argued that only a single-payer system could deliver universal, affordable, and equitable care.

In short, Obama’s former doctor supported single-payer because he believed it was simpler, fairer, and more cost-effective. He opposed the public option because he saw it not as a solution, but as a compromise that left the central flaws of the U.S. health care system intact.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

**Obama’s Evolving Position on Single-Payer Health Care Draws Renewed Scrutiny**

Barack Obama’s position on single-payer health care has long reflected a tension between his stated policy preferences and the political limits he faced as a national candidate and president.

In 2003, while speaking as an Illinois state senator, Obama expressed clear support for a government-run universal health care system. “I happen to be a proponent of a single-payer universal health care program,” Obama said at the time. He added, however, that such a system would require Democratic control and broad political momentum, saying, “We may not get there immediately.”

By the 2008 presidential campaign, Obama’s message had shifted. While he continued to say that single-payer might be the cleanest approach in theory, he argued that the United States could not simply erase the existing employer-based insurance system. “If I were designing a system from scratch, I would probably go ahead with a single-payer system,” Obama said in 2008. But he emphasized that the country was not starting from scratch and that reform had to build on the system already in place.

That shift frustrated some single-payer advocates, including Dr. David Scheiner, Obama’s longtime former physician in Chicago. Scheiner publicly criticized Obama for moving away from the kind of sweeping reform he believed was necessary. Scheiner argued that Obama understood the advantages of single-payer but chose a more politically cautious path once he became a national figure.

The debate came to a head during the push for what became the Affordable Care Act. Rather than pursue Medicare-for-all or another single-payer model, Obama backed a plan centered on private insurance, Medicaid expansion, subsidies, insurance exchanges and new consumer protections. A proposed “public option” — a government-run insurance plan that would compete with private insurers — became the main compromise sought by many liberals.

But even the public option faced strong opposition from Republicans, the insurance industry and moderate Democrats. It was ultimately dropped from the final legislation in order to secure enough votes in the Senate.

Supporters of Obama’s approach say he chose the most realistic path to expand coverage in a closely divided political environment. Critics argue that the decision entrenched private insurers and missed a rare opportunity to fight for a simpler universal system.

The result was a health care law that significantly reduced the uninsured rate and expanded coverage, but left unresolved the broader ideological fight that Obama’s own comments had highlighted years earlier: whether the United States should continue to patch together its mixed public-private system, or move toward single-payer health care.
